newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Venezuela vows to stimulate mining development.
newsitem.headline: Venezuela vows to stimulate mining development.

text.p: Venezuela's Energy and Mines Ministry took control of hundreds of mining contracts and concession applications Monday and vowed to stimulate development in the stalled mining sector.

"Now that the ministry has re-taken control over the granting of concessions it opens a new boom of re-activation in the mining sector," Radames Larazabal, special mining commissioner at the Energy and Mines Ministry told Reuters.
Larazabal spoke after officials from the state-owned holding Corporacion Venezolana de Guayana (CVG) handed over 462 mining contracts and approximately 400 mining applications to the ministry.

The mining contracts were awarded by the CVG between 1991 and 1994. President Rafael Caldera's government halted the CVG's ability to authorize mining concessions and has said they will be turned into concessions.
"We hope that with this impulse to mining...in five years the country could receive $2.5 billion in new investment," Larazabal said.
Mining executives have strongly criticized the Caldera administration for failing to encourage mining development and creating a virtual freeze in the granting of new mining concessions.

Venezuela currently produces about 30 tonnes of gold per year, of which only about 10 tonnes per year is officially registered, Larazabal said. New mining concessions and investments could raise official gold production to between 15 and 20 tonnes per year in five years, he added.
As a means to stimulate gold production, state gold company Minerven, a unit of the CVG, will offer joint ventures with large foreign mining companies, he said.

Minerven, which produces about 7 tonnes of gold for year from its mine at El Callao in south-eastern Venezuela, controls 12 concessions of about 1,250 acres (500 hectares) each. These areas could be developed under joint venture agreements.

The advantage of these joint ventures for the foreign mining partner is that they would by-pass the usual long wait for environmental permits which accompany a new concession application, Larazabal added.

The mining official acknowledged that new mining applications were currently taking between five and 10 years to process and involved about 150 administrative steps often subject to corrupt practices.
"Obviously this nefarious and corrupt practice has to be combatted and eliminated," Larazabal said.
The mining official added that a government proposed mining reform bill appeared to be stalled in Congress but insisted that mining development could still be encouraged under existing legislation.
